disclaimer: This library is a comparison baseline maintained by human reviewers. It is not a statute, not a court ruling, and not a statement that any clause is legal or illegal. Jurisdiction-specific enforceability should be reviewed by a qualified legal professional.

entries.title: Security deposit
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should state the security deposit as a rupee amount or as a defined multiple of rent, and it should not describe that deposit as automatically forfeited.
expected_elements: A stated deposit amount or multiple of rent
missing_elements: Stated deposit amount or multiple of rent

element_checks.description: The deposit is a stated amount or a stated multiple of rent

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag a deposit clause when it forfeits the deposit outright. Stating a multiple of rent, by itself, matches this comparison standard.
entries.financial_basis: The deposit figure is an input to other clauses. Do not treat the mere statement of the deposit as a loss.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant shall pay a security deposit of a stated amount before possession. The deposit remains the tenant's money except for itemized deductions permitted in this agreement.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the deposit amount explicit and remove any automatic forfeiture.
entries.why_it_matters: The deposit is the sum later clauses may put at stake, so the agreement needs a clear figure and no automatic forfeiture.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Damage deductions
entries.standard_expectation: Damage deductions should define damage, exclude normal wear and tear, follow a joint inspection, and be itemized. The comparison standard does not treat a right to keep the entire deposit for undefined damage as aligned.
expected_elements: A distinction from normal wear and tear

element_checks.description: Normal wear and tear is excluded
An inspection is required before a deduction

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag this clause when it lets the owner keep the deposit for damage that the clause does not define, or when the clause allows retention of the entire deposit without itemization and an inspection.
entries.financial_basis: If the clause permits retention of the entire security deposit, potential exposure is the deposit amount. That figure is a maximum relevant asset, not a prediction of loss.
entries.suggested_revision: Deductions shall be itemised following a joint inspection within 7 days of vacating, and the remaining balance shall be refunded within 30 days. Damage means loss beyond normal wear and tear.
entries.negotiation_goal: Replace undefined whole-deposit retention with itemized deductions after a joint inspection.
entries.why_it_matters: The clause can put the whole deposit at stake for a word it does not define, and it does not require an inspection or an itemized list.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Inspection
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should set a joint move-out inspection and a signed note of condition before any deposit deduction.
entries.comparison_guidance: Treat the inspection topic as missing when none of the presence indicators appear in the agreement.
entries.financial_basis: An inspection clause usually has no separate rupee figure. Its absence matters because it removes the process that should support a deposit deduction.
entries.suggested_revision: The owner and the tenant shall carry out a joint inspection within 7 days of vacating, and both parties shall sign the inspection note before any deposit deduction.
entries.negotiation_goal: Add a joint inspection before any deduction from the deposit.
entries.why_it_matters: The agreement does not set a joint inspection before a deposit deduction.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a statement that a particular inspection timeline is legally mandatory.

entries.title: Security deposit return timeline
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should say when the remaining security deposit must be returned after move-out, after any itemized deductions.
entries.comparison_guidance: Treat the return timeline as missing when the agreement never states when the remaining deposit comes back.
entries.financial_basis: No separate amount is invented for a missing timeline. The related exposure, if any, is the deposit figure already stated in the agreement.
entries.suggested_revision: Any remaining security deposit shall be refunded within 30 days of the tenant vacating the premises, after itemized deductions.
entries.negotiation_goal: Add a clear date for return of the remaining deposit.
entries.why_it_matters: The agreement does not specify when the remaining security deposit must be returned.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. The 30-day wording is a proposed comparison revision, not a claim that 30 days is legally required.

entries.title: Itemized deductions
entries.standard_expectation: Deposit deductions should be listed item by item, with an amount for each item, after inspection.
entries.comparison_guidance: Itemization is checked as an expected element of a damage or deduction clause. It is not reported again as a standalone missing clause when that clause is already flagged.
entries.financial_basis: Itemization changes how a deduction is explained. It does not by itself create a new rupee figure.
entries.suggested_revision: Any deduction from the security deposit shall be itemised in writing, with the amount and reason for each item.
entries.negotiation_goal: Require an itemized list before any deduction.
entries.why_it_matters: Without an itemized list, a deduction cannot be matched to a specific item of loss.
entries.source_notes: Applied through STD-DAMAGE-001 so the same gap is not counted twice. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Normal wear and tear
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should define normal wear and tear and should keep ordinary use outside damage deductions.
expected_elements: A definition of normal wear and tear
missing_elements: Definition of normal wear and tear
contradiction_indicators: wear and tear shall be charged in full
entries.comparison_guidance: Flag only if the clause charges the tenant for ordinary wear. A definition of wear and tear matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: No amount is assumed for ordinary wear.
entries.suggested_revision: Normal wear and tear means deterioration from ordinary use and shall not be deducted from the security deposit.
entries.negotiation_goal: Define wear and tear and exclude it from deposit deductions.
entries.why_it_matters: A missing wear-and-tear definition leaves ordinary use open to being treated as damage.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Monthly rent
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should state the monthly rent in rupees and when it is due.
expected_elements: A due date or payment cycle

element_checks.description: Monthly rent is a stated amount

contradiction_indicators: rent as the owner decides from month to month
entries.comparison_guidance: A stated monthly rent and due date match this standard. Do not flag a rent clause only because the amount is large.
entries.financial_basis: Monthly rent is an input to formulas such as months of rent. It is not, by itself, an unusual-clause exposure.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant shall pay a stated monthly rent on a stated day each month.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the rent amount and the due date explicit.
entries.why_it_matters: Other clauses convert months of rent into rupees only if the monthly rent is stated.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Rent escalation
entries.standard_expectation: Any rent increase should be a stated percentage or rupee amount on a stated date.

element_checks.description: The increase is a stated percentage or amount

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag escalation only when the increase is left to discretion or has no figure. A stated percentage on an anniversary matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Exposure is the stated percentage times monthly rent, and only when that percentage is written in the clause. Do not invent a future increase.
entries.suggested_revision: Monthly rent shall increase by a stated percentage on each anniversary, and not otherwise.
entries.negotiation_goal: Replace an open-ended increase with a stated percentage and date.
entries.why_it_matters: An increase without a figure has no defensible rupee value.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Early termination
entries.standard_expectation: If early termination compensation is charged, the comparison standard expects a defined formula that does not exceed one month of rent, after the notice period.
expected_elements: A cap of one month of rent
A link to the notice period
missing_elements: Cap of one month of rent

element_checks.description: Compensation does not exceed one month of rent

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag early termination when compensation is two or more months of rent. One month of rent matches this comparison standard. This cap is a comparison baseline, not a legal limit.
entries.financial_basis: Exposure is the stated multiple times the monthly rent in the agreement. Python multiplies those figures. Do not add a further penalty that is not written down.
entries.suggested_revision: If the tenant terminates during the lock-in period after giving the agreed notice, early-termination compensation shall not exceed one month's rent.
entries.negotiation_goal: Cap early-termination compensation at one month of rent and keep the notice period in place.
entries.why_it_matters: A multiple of rent is a definite exit cost, even when the sentence sounds like a routine condition.
entries.source_notes: The one-month cap is the ClauseLens comparison baseline, not a claim about statutory damages.

entries.title: Notice period
entries.standard_expectation: Ending the agreement should require a stated period of prior written notice.

element_checks.description: Notice is written and has a length

entries.comparison_guidance: A stated written notice period matches this standard. Do not flag it because the number of days could have been different.
entries.financial_basis: Notice by itself has no rupee exposure unless another clause prices a failure to give notice.
entries.suggested_revision: Either party may end this agreement by giving a stated period of prior written notice.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep a clear written notice period.
entries.why_it_matters: Notice is the process for ending the tenancy without surprise.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a claim that a particular number of days is legally mandatory.

entries.title: Lock-in period
entries.standard_expectation: Any lock-in should state its length and point to the early-termination clause that applies during that period.
expected_elements: A pointer to the exit clause
entries.comparison_guidance: A stated lock-in length matches this standard. Price the exit only under the early-termination standard.
entries.financial_basis: The lock-in length is not multiplied into a rupee exposure unless the early-termination clause states a formula.
entries.suggested_revision: The lock-in period is a stated number of months. Exit during that period follows the early-termination clause.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the lock-in length explicit and tie the exit cost to a capped formula.
entries.why_it_matters: An unstated lock-in makes the tenant's ability to leave unclear.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Maintenance
entries.standard_expectation: Structural repairs should sit with the owner. Day-to-day upkeep may sit with the tenant. The tenant should not be given unlimited structural repairs.

element_checks.description: Structural and day-to-day duties are split

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag maintenance only when the tenant is given structural or unlimited repair duties.
entries.financial_basis: Unlimited repair duties have no defensible amount. Do not invent a repair bill.
entries.suggested_revision: The owner is responsible for structural repairs. The tenant is responsible for day-to-day upkeep.
entries.negotiation_goal: Split structural repairs from day-to-day upkeep.
entries.why_it_matters: Unlimited repair language has no ceiling that can be calculated from the agreement.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Utilities
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should say which utilities the tenant pays and which the owner pays.
expected_elements: Owner charges such as property tax where mentioned
entries.comparison_guidance: A clause that names who pays electricity, water, and property tax matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Do not invent a utility bill. Exposure is unknown unless the agreement states an amount or a formula.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant shall pay metered electricity and water. The owner shall pay property tax and society charges unless a schedule states otherwise.
entries.negotiation_goal: Name who pays each utility.
entries.why_it_matters: Unassigned utilities can become a charge with no formula in the agreement.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Repairs
entries.standard_expectation: The tenant should notify the owner of defects, and the owner should repair structural defects.

element_checks.description: Defects are notified and structural repairs sit with the owner

contradiction_indicators: tenant shall carry out all structural repairs
entries.comparison_guidance: Flag repairs only when structural work is placed entirely on the tenant.
entries.financial_basis: No repair invoice is invented.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant shall notify the owner of defects in writing. The owner shall repair structural defects.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep structural repairs with the owner.
entries.why_it_matters: Structural repairs can be expensive, and the agreement should say who performs them.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Painting
entries.standard_expectation: Normal repainting at the end of the term should not be an automatic tenant charge.
contradiction_indicators: tenant shall repaint the entire premises at the tenant's cost regardless of condition
entries.comparison_guidance: A clause that excuses normal end-of-term repainting matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Do not invent a painting quote.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant is not charged for normal repainting at the end of the term. Painting required by damage beyond normal wear may be itemized.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep ordinary repainting off the tenant's bill.
entries.why_it_matters: An automatic full repaint can become a move-out charge with no price in the agreement.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Cleaning
entries.standard_expectation: Move-out cleaning should be a defined standard such as broom-clean, with ordinary use excepted.
contradiction_indicators: professional cleaning at a cost fixed by the owner later
entries.comparison_guidance: A broom-clean standard with ordinary use excepted matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Do not invent a cleaning invoice when no fee is stated.
entries.suggested_revision: The tenant shall leave the premises in broom-clean condition, fair wear from ordinary use excepted.
entries.negotiation_goal: Use a defined cleaning standard instead of an open-ended fee.
entries.why_it_matters: An undefined cleaning charge has no amount until a fee is written down.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Late payment
entries.standard_expectation: A late fee should be a stated amount, should follow a grace period, and should have a cap.
contradiction_indicators: late fee at the owner's discretion
entries.comparison_guidance: A stated daily fee with a grace period and a cap matches this standard. Do not flag it because the wording is firm.
entries.financial_basis: If a cap is stated, the potential exposure of a late-fee clause is the cap, not an open-ended count of days. If there is a daily rate and no cap and no stated number of days, exposure is unknown.
entries.suggested_revision: A late fee of a stated amount per day applies after a stated grace period and is capped at a stated amount per month.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the late fee stated, delayed by a grace period, and capped.
entries.why_it_matters: An uncapped daily fee has no maximum that can be calculated.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Renewal
entries.standard_expectation: Renewal should say who may propose it and how long before expiry the proposal is made.
contradiction_indicators: renewal only at a rent the owner will set later with no formula
entries.comparison_guidance: A written renewal proposal with a stated lead time matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Renewal has no exposure unless a new rent formula is stated.
entries.suggested_revision: Either party may propose renewal in writing a stated number of days before expiry.
entries.negotiation_goal: State how renewal is proposed.
entries.why_it_matters: Silence on renewal leaves the next term's rent and notice unsettled.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Subletting
entries.standard_expectation: Subletting should be either permitted on stated conditions or refused unless the owner gives prior written consent.
entries.comparison_guidance: A prior-written-consent rule matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: No penalty is invented for a consent rule that states no fee.
entries.suggested_revision: Subletting is not permitted without the owner's prior written consent.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the consent rule explicit and free of an undefined penalty.
entries.why_it_matters: An undefined subletting penalty has no calculable amount.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Administrative charge
entries.standard_expectation: A move-in or administrative charge, if any, should be a stated fee. Non-payment of that fee alone should not be described as a material breach.
expected_elements: No material-breach trigger for that fee alone
missing_elements: Stated administrative charge, if one is intended

element_checks.description: The fee is a stated amount

entries.comparison_guidance: Flag an administrative charge when non-payment is a material breach or when the charge is described as non-refundable and punitive. Absence of an administrative charge is not a missing protection.
entries.financial_basis: Exposure is the stated fee in the clause. Do not add termination damages that the clause does not price.
entries.suggested_revision: Any administrative charge shall be a stated amount payable on signing, and non-payment of that charge alone shall not be a material breach.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep any admin fee as a stated amount and remove the material-breach trigger.
entries.why_it_matters: The fee may be small, but calling non-payment a material breach raises consequences the fee itself does not price.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement. Not reported as missing when the agreement simply has no admin fee.

entries.title: Key return
entries.standard_expectation: A key-return charge should be a stated fee and should follow a short grace period. A one-day delay should not be described as a serious default.
missing_elements: Grace period before a key-return charge
entries.comparison_guidance: Flag a key clause when delay is a serious default or the tenant bears the charge at their sole peril. A stated fee with a grace period matches this standard. Absence of a key clause is not a missing protection.
entries.financial_basis: Exposure is the stated key fee. Do not add an extra penalty that is not priced.
entries.suggested_revision: If the keys are not returned within 2 days after vacating, the tenant shall pay the stated key charge and no further sum for that delay.
entries.negotiation_goal: Keep the key fee stated, add a short grace period, and remove serious-default language.
entries.why_it_matters: The stated fee is the only defensible amount. Serious-default wording is a comparison difference even when the fee is small.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.

entries.title: Brokerage
entries.standard_expectation: The agreement should say whether the tenant owes brokerage.
contradiction_indicators: brokerage at a rate the broker will decide later
entries.comparison_guidance: A statement that no brokerage is payable, or a stated brokerage fee, matches this standard.
entries.financial_basis: Use a stated brokerage fee if one appears. Do not invent a commission.
entries.suggested_revision: No brokerage is payable by the tenant under this agreement.
entries.negotiation_goal: State whether brokerage is payable and, if it is, the amount.
entries.why_it_matters: An unstated brokerage claim has no figure in the agreement.
entries.source_notes: ClauseLens comparison baseline v1.0.0. Not a legal requirement.
